definition: Pugnacious means quarrelsome; eager to pick a fight.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pugnacious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pugnacious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The startup stayed pugnacious long after it grew up, suing two giants and picking a public fight with its own industry group in a single quarter.
Feisty is spirited pushback with a wink in it; pugnacious genuinely wants the quarrel.
Violent goes past pugnacious — past wanting the fight, into doing the damage.

Belligerent is openly warlike — hostile and ready for the real thing, a step past pugnacious. The pugnacious love the quarrel itself and can even be likable in their eagerness; the belligerent have stopped enjoying and started threatening. One picks fights; the other means war.

Scrappy is the admiring word for a fighter's spirit without the picked quarrels — all-out effort, fearless hustle, no grudge and no dispute anywhere. Pugnacious wants the quarrel itself; the scrappy player just wants the loose ball, and would rather win than argue.

Pugnacious means quarrelsome; eager to pick a fight.
Bruno is six, and the karate school has met no one so pugnacious.
He challenged the instructor on day one, then the assistant, then a heavy bag he judged to be looking at him.
His gi is too big and his stance is terrible, and every Saturday he asks, hopefully, whether today is the day they spar for real.
Pugnacious is the exact word because it names the appetite for the fight itself — quarrelsome, combative, leading with the chin.
Bruno isn't angry at anyone and holds no grudges; he simply wants the bout.
That eagerness, comic in a six-year-old and alarming in a CEO, is pugnacity in its purest form.
Pugnacious is for the fight-seekers — people, animals, and institutions that treat the quarrel as the point.
Its cluster in this unit splits cleanly: contentious disputes claims, fractious is irritable and unsteerable, but pugnacious wants the bout itself.
Said with a smile it can even admire — a pugnacious little boxer of a word.

Alderman Petrosky had served six terms, and no one could remember a quiet one.
He was pugnacious by nature: he had picked a public quarrel with the parks department, the water board, and, one memorable spring, the state's official mapmakers.
The quarrels rarely came to anything, and he never seemed to mind.
Colleagues noticed he was cheerful for days after starting one.
'He doesn't want to win,' the council clerk said.
Winning would only end it.' When a reporter asked if he planned to mellow in his seventh term, Petrosky said he had his eye on the county fair committee, and smiled.
